description: We're Computer Science students from Unioeste (Brazil) taking on the "Equipment on the Moon and Mars" challenge.
summary:
In 1967 a small lander touched down on the Moon. In 1972 a probe left Earth, headed for Jupiter, and kept going. In 2004, twin rollers rolled off its lander on Mars, built to last ninety days. It lasted almost fifteen years.

Then, one after another, they went quiet. They're still out there.

I'm Still Here is a short, story-driven game about those three machines: Surveyor 3, Pioneer 10 and the twins Spirit and Opportunity. Each chapter takes about four to seven minutes. You play as the rovers, reliving their mission's most memorable moments. You fly, drive and dig with them, use the same instruments their teams used, and find out why it mattered that they went at all. And you're there at the end, when each of them sent its last signal home.

They stopped talking a long time ago. We wanted to give them one more chance to be heard
details:
Some explorers never came home.

I'm Still Here is a cinematic, story-driven game that lets young space fans relive the final missions of NASA hardware still out in the Solar System. It runs in a web browser, with nothing to install, and is told in three chapters of about five to seven minutes each.

In the first, Surveyor 3 lands on the Moon in 1967 to test whether its soil could hold a crewed landing. In the second, Pioneer 10 crosses the asteroid belt, passes Jupiter and heads for the stars carrying a message for whoever finds it. In the third, the twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity land on opposite sides of Mars and search the rocks for signs of ancient water.

Instead of reading about these machines, players become them. Short cinematic scenes set up each moment, then the player takes control: digging into lunar soil, piecing together a picture of Jupiter, grinding into a Martian rock and reading what the instruments find inside. Every interaction is built around a real instrument and what it actually measured. And you're there at the end, when each of them sent its last signal home.

We built the game in Unity 6 with C# and the Universal Render Pipeline, and exported it to WebGL so it runs on ordinary school computers. Mission facts, dates, landing coordinates, archive images and most of the 3D models come from NASA, JPL and NASA GISS Mars24. We used AI tools along the way: an AI coding assistant (Claude) helped write and test parts of the game code, several 3d models were generated with ChatGPT and one song was AI-generated. Every AI-assisted piece was reviewed by the team, every fact was checked against NASA sources, and all narration is recorded by people.

We designed for kids around 10 to 15 years old and for anyone curious about space. The controls are simple: move, and hold one key to act. There are no fail states, the game offers help when a player gets stuck, and subtitles are available in English and Portuguese.

Most young people only hear about the missions flying today. These older machines did the groundwork for everything that followed, and they're still out there, silent. I'm Still Here gives them one more chance to be heard, and we hope it gives players a reason to look up and wonder what's next.

Heads up: I'm Still Here uses 3D graphics and runs entirely in your browser, so some older or low-end computers may not run it smoothly or show every effect. If the game stutters, try closing other tabs and apps, using a recent version of Chrome, Edge or Firefox, and making sure your browser's hardware acceleration is turned on.

Github link: https://github.com/joaovdamaceno/AbandonedButNotForgotten-SpaceApps
